content: In optics, a virtual image is an image where the outgoing light rays from a point on the object do not actually converge at a single point. A common example of this is the image seen in a flat mirror. When you look into a flat mirror, the image of yourself appears to be located at a distance behind the mirror equal to the distance you are in front of it. For instance, if you stand 0.5 meters in front of the mirror, your image will appear to be 0.5 meters behind the mirror. In contrast, a real image is formed when the outgoing light rays from a point on the object physically converge at a single point. Real images are most easily observed when projected onto an opaque screen, although the screen itself is not necessary for the image to exist. For example, when you observe a focused image on a screen placed behind a converging lens (a lens with at least one convex surface) or in front of a concave mirror, the image is real because the light rays actually converge at the location of the screen. If the screen is removed, the real image can still be observed by positioning yourself such that the image appears to be located at the same point in space. When looking through a diverging lens (a lens with at least one concave surface) or into a convex mirror, the image you see is a virtual image. Similarly, a converging lens or a concave mirror can also produce virtual images if the object is located within the focal length of the optical device. For example, a plane mirror or a convex mirror forms a virtual image that appears to be located behind the mirror. Although the light rays seem to originate from behind the mirror, the actual light from the source only exists in front of the mirror and spreads outward. In diagrams of optical systems, virtual rays are conventionally represented by dotted lines. These virtual rays indicate the perceived paths of light as seen by an observer looking into the optical device. However, the light does not physically travel along these dotted paths. A point on the virtual image is defined as the location where these virtual rays appear to intersect.
